newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's lower inflation target at risk - official.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's lower inflation target at risk - official.

text.p: Servet Yildirim

A senior economy official has acknowledged Turkey may have to revise upward its 1997 inflation target after first quarter results, released last week, showed no improvement for the deficit-ridden economy.
"The inflation target might be revised," Treasury Undersecretary Mehmet Kaytaz told a business meeting on Thursday night.
"Inflation was high in the first three months of this year," Kaytaz said.

Turkey reported wholesale price inflation for the first quarter at 19 percent, putting in doubt its annual target of 57.5 percent. Inflation was 24 percent for the same quarter in 1996 and 78 percent for all of last year.

All the same, Kaytaz said, the government's economic programme -- built around a sharp increase in privatisation revenues -- may nonetheless help offset high inflation that has gripped Turkey for two decades.
Economists say inflation will remain high unless the government closes its high budget deficit, which reached more than eight percent of the gross national product last year.

Most have dismissed as unrealistic the government's 1997 target for a zero-deficit budget, questioning the underlying assumption of transfers worth $4.5 billion from the sell-off of Turk Telekom and licence sale revenues to the consolidated budget.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and his deputy Tansu Ciller announced earlier that preliminary 1997 data signalled their budget remained on target.
But economists believe the government, which has yet to announce any official budget deficit figures, is using accounting tricks.

"I don't know what the budget deficit was in the first three months," said Kaytaz, whose duties include financing any shortfall. He blamed the finance ministry for delays in the announcement of budget figures.
The treasury has borrowed 2,567 trillion lira from the domestic markets this year, raising the domestic debt stock to 3,605 trillion lira as of end-February.
Kaytaz said Turkey should ease the burden on the economy of its domestic debt stock, now around 15 percent of the GNP.
"But there is no miraculous way. Turkey must pay a price and bear its cost to do this," he added.
Economists say Turkey should rely more on foreign borrowing to relieve domestic debt pressures.

The treasury services around $7.5 billion of external debt a year. It raised around $2.8 billion from the international capital markets and secured about $2 billion of long-term project financing last year.
The gap was financed through domestic borrowing at very high real rates.
"We should be a net foreign borrower instead of net payer. But downgradings of our credit rating have affected our cost of borrowing," Kaytaz said.
Bankers say Turkey's sub-investment sovereign ratings -- B from Standard and Poor's and B1 from Moody's -- weaken its ability to borrow more from foreign debt markets at reasonable rates.
Under these constraints, the government has been forced to rely heavily on privatisation to correct its badly-shaken fiscal position, one of the major reasons behind credit rating cuts.
Turkey has concluded $553 million of privatisation deals so far this year. The privatisation administration will raise $233 million in cash this year out of these deals.

The government appointed a Goldman Sachs-led consortium as adviser to speed up its efforts to privatise Turk Telekom -- the lynchpin of the 10-year-old sell-off programme -- and to raise $3.3 billion this year.
"The government is determined to accelerate sell-offs. But it may be hard to complete the Telekom privatisation by the end of this year," Kaytaz said.
